paras: The attempted lynching of Joe Milton took place at Cheneyville, Rapides Parish, Louisiana, on the night of August 10, 1900, when an armed white mob hunted down and captured Milton, a Black man accused of killing a young white man, Bennie Wall. The sheriff refused to allow a lynching, and Milton was jailed at Alexandria, where he died days later. The case drew national notice mainly because a mass meeting of white residents then ordered idle Black men to leave town.

According to a New Orleans special to the New-York Tribune, Wall and Samuel Blum met Milton and his "sweetheart" on a narrow plankwalk between Cheneyville and "Theoda." In that account Milton brushed against Wall, Wall struck him, and both men drew revolvers and fired four shots each. Wall was shot in the abdomen and died within minutes, while one of his bullets broke Milton's leg.

Other papers told the start differently: the Weekly Iberian said Wall knocked Milton down for "jostling" him, and the Lafayette Gazette said Milton "disputed" Wall's right of way. The first report, in the Age-Herald, named the man "Joseph Hamilton" and gave no cause.

Milton crawled into a field, and the news gathered what a traveler writing to the Weekly Iberian called "an armed mob bent on finishing up the negro." The writer, who was at the depot that evening, described the mob following the track of Milton's broken leg by lantern, Milton emptying his revolver at them, and a fusillade that marked his capture. As Milton lay on the depot platform, a few men argued against killing him and "angry numbers" argued for it.

Armed squads from Bunkie, Alexandria, Lamourie and other places also rode in to offer help, according to the New Orleans wire. The sheriff of Rapides Parish "stood firm in his determination to allow no lynching" and sent them away, and Milton was carried to jail at Alexandria.

Within days the white residents held a mass meeting, chaired by C. Cannon, on a Saturday by the Iberian's account and a Sunday by the Thibodaux Sentinel's. Its resolutions told Black men with "no visible means of gaining a livelihood" to find work or be compelled to leave, pledged to break up gambling places, ordered pistols taken, and barred sitting on the depot steps. Young Black people who failed to yield sidewalks to white "ladies and children" were to be "severely dealt with," while nine-tenths of the Black population were called "law-abiding and worthy" and promised protection.

A committee of twenty-two at once closed places where Black residents gathered and warned idle men to leave, and the wire reported that "Quite an emigration set in at once." The Tribune reported that Milton died after an operation on his leg; the Lafayette Gazette said he died of his wounds. No report of an inquest or of action against the mob appears in the coverage.

All the coverage found comes from white newspapers. The Tribune headlined its first story "Race Difficulty Leads to Bloodshed" and blamed "the incompatibility of the white and black races." The August 13 wire, headed "To Regulate Negroes' Conduct" in the New York Sun and "Whites Regulate Blacks" in the Washington Times, quoted the resolutions without comment and noted the town's link to "Uncle Tom's Cabin." It was reprinted in Virginia, North Carolina and Iowa papers on August 15 and 16.

Louisiana weeklies endorsed the meeting. The Weekly Iberian headlined its item "Another Bad Coon," praised Cheneyville's "cool judgment" in not lynching, and warned that idle men who did not reform "will be driven out as would vicious be dogs." The Lafayette Gazette called the resolutions "conservative," and the Thibodaux Sentinel wrote that Wall was "brutally murdered by a negro of the Robert Charles type." The New-York Tribune, by contrast, ridiculed the resolutions' "wonderfully and fearfully bad grammar."
The Age-Herald dispatch and the Iberian letter place the shooting on Friday, August 10, while the Tribune special and the Iberian editorial give August 11.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Milton and the Cheneyville resolutions
bases: An armed white mob hunted, shot at and captured the wounded Joe Milton and argued over killing him before he was jailed (A2, A10, A11); the attempt was followed by a mass meeting that ordered idle Black men to leave town and set rules for Black residents (A3, A5, A12).

An armed mob pursued and captured Milton intending to kill him for the killing of Wall, but he was jailed at Alexandria (A2, A10, A11); he later died, of an operation on his leg according to the Tribune and of his gunshot wounds according to the Lafayette Gazette, not at the mob's hands (A5, A13).
A New Orleans special, a separate New Orleans wire, a Louisiana traveler's letter and a Louisiana editorial independently report the shooting, the mob and the averted lynching (A2, A3, A10, A11).

accounts.label: First wire report
accounts.gist: Wall was shot and killed by a Black man, 'Joseph Hamilton', whose leg was broken by Wall's bullet; Hamilton was arrested and the cause was unknown.

accounts.label: New Orleans special to the Tribune
accounts.gist: Milton brushed against Wall on a narrow plankwalk, Wall struck him, both drew revolvers and fired four shots each; an enraged white crowd gathered and a lynching was averted only with great difficulty.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire of Aug. 13
accounts.gist: Armed squads from surrounding towns rode in to help lynch Milton but the sheriff refused; white residents then met and adopted rules for Black residents, enforced by a committee of twenty-two.

accounts.label: Traveler's letter to the Weekly Iberian
accounts.gist: An armed mob trailed Milton by lantern through a cane field, he emptied his revolver at them, he was captured amid a fusillade, and the crowd argued on the depot platform over killing him.

accounts.label: Louisiana weeklies
accounts.gist: Wall knocked Milton down for 'jostling' him or Milton 'disputed' Wall's right of way on the sidewalk; the Lafayette Gazette says Milton died of his wounds.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'Race Difficulty Leads to Bloodshed' and blamed 'the incompatibility of the white and black races', reported the averted lynching, and later mocked the resolutions' 'fearfully bad grammar'.
The Aug. 13 wire ran as 'To Regulate Negroes' Conduct' or 'Whites Regulate Blacks' and quoted the resolutions without comment, closing on Cheneyville's link to 'Uncle Tom's Cabin'.
The Weekly Iberian headlined 'Another Bad Coon', praised Cheneyville for not lynching and said idle Black men who did not reform would be 'driven out as would vicious be dogs'.
The Lafayette Gazette called the resolutions 'conservative' and fit for many Louisiana towns; the Thibodaux Sentinel called Milton 'a negro of the Robert Charles type'.

conflicts.note: Only the earliest brief report uses Hamilton; every later and fuller account uses Milton.

The Age-Herald dispatch is datelined Aug. 10 'this afternoon' and the Iberian letter writer, who was present, says Friday evening (Aug. 10); the Tribune special dated Aug. 11 says 'to-day', perhaps the filing date.
Both fall before the Aug. 13 New Orleans wire.
